disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more discrete episodes of at least two weeks in which there is a pervasive change in mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure, accompanied by a constellation of cognitive, somatic, and behavioral changes that cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Typical presentations include persistent low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite changes, psychomotor changes, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide. Episodes can be precipitated by psychosocial stressors but may also arise without a clear external trigger, and the course ranges from single episodes to recurrent, sometimes chronic, patterns. MDD is distinguished from bipolar disorders by the absence of manic or hypomanic episodes, and from normal grief or adjustment reactions by the severity, breadth of impairment, and persistence of symptoms.

narrative.stressor: About six months into his retirement, Cyntrell began noticing increasing forgetfulness and minor lapses in attention—misplacing tools, leaving the stove on, losing his train of thought while mentoring teens at the maker space. His primary care doctor raised concerns about possible mild cognitive impairment, ordered neurocognitive testing, and recommended that he cut back on driving and certain independent activities until results were clearer, which Cyntrell experienced as a direct challenge to the competence and self-reliance that had defined his identity as an engineer and community mentor. Over the following weeks, he gradually withdrew from church choir and woodworking projects, and his carefully planned fishing trips and heritage tours stopped as he fixated on the possibility of “losing his mind,” straining his relationship with his wife, who became increasingly anxious and protective. After roughly three weeks of marked decline in his day-to-day functioning—neglecting his garden, canceling mentorship sessions, and sitting for long periods without engaging in his usual hobbies—his pastor and wife jointly encouraged him to see a mental health professional, leading to psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just don’t feel like doing any of the things I used to love—my workshop, church, even fishing don’t mean anything to me right now.”

narrative.stressor: In the aftermath of a particularly intense hurricane season, Desserie’s community clinic became chronically understaffed, and she found herself working extended shifts while also studying for her RN-to-BSN bridge program entrance exams. Initially, she tried to channel the pressure into her usual outlets—painting, yoga, and leading community health-and-art workshops—but over several weeks the combination of vicarious trauma from displaced patients, administrative demands, and her own high expectations eroded her sense of purpose at work. When she received notice that her first attempt at a key certification exam had been unsuccessful, she interpreted it as proof that she was failing both her patients and her long-term goals, and she quietly began pulling back from friends, salsa nights, and even family gatherings in Río Grande. After three weeks of feeling increasingly overwhelmed and preoccupied with dark thoughts about whether her efforts to help others were even worthwhile, she scared herself one night by catching how much time she’d spent online reading about death and methods of self-harm, and a trusted supervisor urged her to seek urgent psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep thinking about death, and I’m starting to worry about the thoughts I’m having about not wanting to be here anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Janio’s rotating night shifts at the casino increasingly conflicted with his wife’s daytime work schedule and their young child’s school routine, leaving them with little overlapping family time. A recent dispute about whether to move closer to his in-laws to get more childcare support escalated into ongoing tension at home, and his wife began commenting that he was emotionally checked out and "never really present" even when he was physically there. During a particularly busy month at work, he started spending his off-hours alone rather than cooking family meals or playing guitar with his child, and he noticed that he would sit staring at the TV unable to follow the plot of shows he used to enjoy or concentrate long enough to finish his crosswords. After about three weeks of this pattern affecting his ability to stay focused on the CCTV monitors and increasing arguments with his wife about his "zoning out," he grew worried that his mental state was putting both his job performance and marriage at risk, prompting him to schedule an appointment with a psychiatrist recommended by his primary care doctor.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind feels foggy all the time—I can’t focus at work or even finish a simple puzzle like I used to.”
